title: The Year Without a Summer: 1816 and the World Tambora Made
subtitle: 1816 and the World Tambora Made
description: In April 1815, Mount Tambora erupted with unprecedented force, shrouding the planet in ash and stealing the following summer. Snow fell on New England in June; famine stalked Ireland and Switzerland; cholera surged from Bengal; and a sunless Geneva inspired Frankenstein. Yet those enduring the cold, hunger, and disease never knew a volcano was to blame. This narrative reconstructs 1816 as a global panorama, tracing the eruption’s invisible shockwaves through weather diaries, parish registers, and price lists across four continents. From Yunnan’s failed rice harvests to American frontier migrations and Parisian bread riots, it reveals a pre-industrial world far more interconnected than previously understood. The volcanic science is established early, then yields to the human experience of a climate catastrophe whose cause remained a mystery to its victims. A vivid chronicle of resilience and ruin, this history illuminates how a single geological event reshaped societies, economies, and cultures long before the modern age of globalization.

editorReview.text: This panoramic account of the Tambora eruption's global aftermath delivers on its geographical promise, tracing the volcanic veil from Sumbawa to Vermont with documented specificity. Its strongest moments, like the sensory immersion of Chapter 1 or the insightful analysis of how artists like Turner gave form to the 'ambient dread,' elevate the chronicle. However, the narrative drive is periodically fractured by repetitive structural formulas, particularly in chapter openings, which can create a sense of déjà vu rather than deepening momentum.
